transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, uh, thanks for seeing me. I guess what brings me in is... well, I'm an electrician, right? And lately, I keep going back over my jobs again and again. Like, checking the breakers, making sure the labels are perfectly straight, re-checking the torque marks... I even take photos on my phone of the panel before I leave. Which reminds me, my phone ran out of storage the other day because of all the pictures. I had to go down to the AT&T store, and you know how long that takes. The guy there, I think his name was Gary, tried to sell me on this huge cloud storage plan, but I don't trust the cloud. My buddy Dave lost all his vacation photos on the cloud once. Anyway, where was I? Oh, right, the jobs. Yeah, sometimes I even drive back to a site after I've clocked out just to make sure I didn't miss anything. It's making a simple install take way longer than it should, and... well, the guys on the crew and my boss are starting to notice.
Do you feel anxious or upset when you're not able to check your work as many times as you want?

Yeah, definitely. If I can't go back and check... man, my stomach just ties itself in knots. Like I was saying, I just keep going over these jobs again and again, and if somebody stops me from looking at the breakers or making sure the labels are straight, I get really on edge. 

Like last week, my foreman, Frank, told me to just lock up the panel and leave because we were behind. We were at this big commercial build over on Elm Street. Parking there is a complete joke, by the way. You have to park three blocks away and lug your tool bag the whole way, and the meter maids around there are ruthless. I got a sixty-dollar ticket last month just because my back tire was barely touching the red zone. Can you believe that? Sixty bucks! I tried to appeal it online, but their website is straight out of the nineties and keeps crashing. 

But yeah, if I can't do my checks, or if I can't drive back to the site to make sure I didn't miss anything, it just eats at me. I can't focus on the next job, and it just makes everything take way longer than it should.
Do you have any routines or habits outside of your job that you feel like you have to do over and over?

Outside of work? Uh, no, not really. I mean, I don't think so. Once I'm off the clock and away from the panels, I don't have that same urge to keep checking things. I usually just head home and try to relax, maybe watch some TV. 

Actually, I just got one of those new OLED TVs last weekend. Best Buy was having a massive sale. You know the one over on Route 9? The traffic getting into that plaza is always a complete nightmare right now because they’re doing all that construction on the overpass. They’ve been working on that bridge for, what, two years now? My buddy Dave—the same guy who lost his photos on the cloud—he operates an excavator for the county, and he says the city just keeps stalling the permits. It's ridiculous where our tax dollars go, you know? You'd think they could finish a simple repaving job in less than a decade. 

But anyway, I finally got the TV set up. The picture quality is insane, but the delivery guys tracked mud all over my living room rug. I spent like an hour trying to scrub it out with this foam cleaner my wife bought... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, habits at home. Yeah, no, I don't really do anything over and over at the house. It's pretty much just the job sites where I get stuck like that.
Are your repetitive checks at work causing problems in your relationships with your crew or boss?

Yeah, it's definitely causing some friction. My business schedule is totally slipping because jobs that I should easily knock out in one visit end up turning into these extra callbacks and checks. It's really starting to cost me client confidence, and honestly, it's taking away time I should be spending with the apprentices. 

Speaking of the apprentices, we got this new kid, Tyler. Good kid, but man, he is glued to his phone. I swear, every time I turn around, he's scrolling through TikTok or something. I asked him to hand me a wire stripper the other day and he handed me a pair of needle-nose pliers because he wasn't even looking. Kids today, right? They just don't have the same work ethic. When I was his age, I was hauling conduit up three flights of stairs in the dead of summer and thanking my boss for the opportunity. 

But yeah, it's bad. I'm even skipping things I used to enjoy after work. I used to go to this bowling league on Thursday nights—we were actually in second place last season. Our team name was the "Spare Me's," kind of cheesy, I know. But I haven't been in weeks because I'm either still tied up reviewing a job or just sitting at home worrying about whether I need to drive back and check a panel. It's just exhausting.
Are you finding it difficult to enjoy or participate in activities you used to like because of your need to check things over and over?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was just saying about the bowling league... I'm just skipping things I used to really enjoy doing after work because I'm either still tied up reviewing a job, or I'm at home just worrying myself sick about whether I need to drive back to a site. 

And it's not just my free time, it's my whole business schedule. It's completely slipping. Jobs I should easily finish in one visit turn into these extra callbacks and checks, and it's starting to cost me client confidence, not to mention the time I should be spending with the apprentices. 

Speaking of clients, I had this one lady recently—Mrs. Gable. Really nice house over in the Heights, but she has this little yappy dog, a Shih Tzu or something, that just barks at your ankles the entire time you're trying to work. I mean, non-stop. I don't know how people live with dogs like that. I grew up with Golden Retrievers, you know? Real dogs. My dad had this Golden named Barnaby who used to carry his own leash in his mouth when it was time for a walk. Smartest dog I ever met. He actually figured out how to open the latch on the screen door on our back porch, so he'd just let himself out whenever he wanted. We had to start locking the main door just to keep him inside during thunderstorms... 

Wait, sorry, I'm rambling. What was the question? But yeah, the checking just ruins my schedule and my free time. I can't really enjoy much of anything right now.
Do you feel like your need to check things over and over is causing you a lot of distress?

Yeah, it really is. It's... it's incredibly stressful. Like I've been saying, it's just wrecking everything. My business schedule is completely slipping. You know, jobs I should finish in one visit are turning into these endless callbacks and extra checks. It's starting to cost me client confidence, and it's eating up the time I'm supposed to be spending with the apprentices. 

And then my personal time is just shot. I've been skipping the bowling league and other things I used to enjoy after work because I'm either still tied up reviewing a job, or I'm at home just... worrying. Just pacing around wondering if I need to drive all the way back out there. 

Speaking of driving, my truck is making this awful grinding noise when I shift into third gear. It's a 2015 F-150, usually runs like a top, but lately... I don't know. I took it to my mechanic, Sal. Sal's a great guy, salt of the earth. He's been working on my cars since I got my license. His shop is over by the old abandoned paper mill. You know that big brick building with the smokestack that got hit by lightning back in '08? Anyway, Sal says it might be the transmission synchronizer, which is going to be a huge pain because parts for that specific year are backordered everywhere. He said he might have to pull one from a salvage yard in upstate New York. I told him, Sal, I can't be without my truck for a week, I've got tools in there, I've got... 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? But yeah, to answer your question, it's causing me a ton of distress. The whole thing is just exhausting.
Are you feeling like your need to check things over and over is significantly impairing your ability to function in daily life?

Like I keep saying, doc, yeah, one hundred percent. I feel like a broken record here, but my whole ability to just get through a normal day is completely messed up. I can't function right when my business schedule is constantly slipping like this. A simple job that should take one visit turns into me doing all these extra checks and endless callbacks. It's seriously costing me the confidence of my clients, and I'm totally neglecting the apprentices I'm supposed to be training. And then after work, I'm skipping everything I actually enjoy doing because I'm either stuck at a site reviewing a job again, or I'm just sitting on my couch worrying if I need to drive back. 

I used to just come home, grab a beer, and maybe prep my gear to go fishing. I've got this great little bass boat, a '98 Tracker. Aluminum hull. Takes an absolute beating but it's perfect for the shallow water out at Lake Miller. Though last time I took it out, the outboard motor was acting up. Kept sputtering every time I gave it some throttle. I'm pretty sure the carburetor is gummed up. You really gotta run ethanol-free gas in those older two-strokes, otherwise the ethanol just eats right through the fuel lines and guncs everything up. I learned that the hard way back when I had my first dirt bike, a Yamaha YZ125. Man, that thing was fast. I wiped out on a gravel road once and scraped all the skin off my left forearm, my mom was absolutely furious... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Right, daily life. But yeah, my daily life is basically just working, checking, and worrying. It's really no way to live.
When you're checking your work over and over, what is it that you're most afraid of finding or what is the worst thing that could happen if you don't check everything?

Honestly, it's always about causing a fire. Even after I know I checked a panel or a disconnect, this thought just keeps barging in on me that maybe I missed one loose neutral or left something that could spark and start a fire. I try to shake it off, you know, tell myself I did the job right, but it just follows me all the way home. 

Fires are no joke. I always tell my clients to make sure they're testing their smoke detectors, but nobody ever changes the batteries. You're supposed to do it when the clocks change. I actually just went to Costco to buy a huge pack of 9-volts for my own house. Man, I love Costco, but you go in there for batteries and come out with a $300 receipt. Last time I went, they had these massive inflatable paddleboards right in the center aisle. I almost bought one, but then I remembered I don't even like swimming in the ocean. The water around here is way too cold anyway, even in August. My wife and I went to Cape Cod a few years ago and the water was absolutely freezing, plus there are all those great white sharks they keep spotting off the coast now. They have an app that tracks them, actually, and you can see...

Wait, sorry, I'm rambling again. But yeah, that's the main fear. I'm just terrified I'll make a mistake that burns a house down, and the thought just won't leave me alone.
When you're checking your work over and over, is it because you're worried you might have made a specific mistake or because you think something might be imperfect?

Well, kind of like I was just saying, it's definitely a specific mistake. I really don't care if the panel looks pretty or if the wire routing is picture-perfect. It's exactly that thing I just mentioned—that thought just barging in that maybe I missed one loose neutral. Even when I know for a fact I checked the disconnect, that fear of leaving something that could spark and start a fire just follows me all the way home. 

Speaking of the drive home, they've been doing all this road work on Route 9, and it is a complete nightmare. They've had the right lane closed for, what, three months now? And the potholes... I hit one so hard last Tuesday I thought I bent a rim on the truck. Tires aren't cheap either, especially the heavy-duty all-terrains I have to buy because some of these new residential construction sites are just pure mud. You get out there after a good rain and you're sinking up to your ankles. I had a brand new pair of Red Wing boots completely ruined that way last spring. Great boots, too. Took me a solid month to break them in, and I had just treated the leather with this mink oil my grandfather used to swear by. He was a cobbler, actually, had a little shop downtown next to the old movie theater before they tore it down to build that pharmacy...

Wait, sorry. I'm way off track again. But no, it's not about perfection at all. It's just that specific fear of a loose wire and a fire.
Do you feel like things need to be in a certain order or symmetrical when you're working on a job?

No, not really. Like I said, I don't care if it looks pretty or if the wires are perfectly straight or whatever. It's just about making sure it's safe. I mean, sure, I like my truck to be organized, but that's just because I hate digging around for a wire nut when I'm up on a ladder. 

Ladders are getting heavier, I swear. I bought this new fiberglass Werner last month, a ten-footer, and hauling that thing off the roof rack is killing my shoulder. I think I slept on it wrong, too. We got this new mattress, one of those memory foam things they ship to you in a box. It's crazy how they vacuum seal it down that small. You cut the plastic and it just inflates like a life raft. My wife loves it, but I feel like I'm sinking into quicksand every night. It gets so hot, too. I end up kicking the blankets off by 2 AM. We used to have a regular spring mattress, had it for like fifteen years, and honestly, I slept way better on that old thing. I tried to tell her we should just flip it, but she said it was sagging...

Uh, what was the question? Order and symmetry? Yeah, no, I don't care about that stuff on the job. Just the fire thing.
Do you feel like checking everything repeatedly helps you regain a sense of control over the situation?

I don't know if I'd call it control, exactly. I mean, I guess I'm just trying to make sure I don't burn a place down. So, no, it's not really about feeling in control, it's just trying to stop that bad feeling from happening. 

Speaking of feeling in control, though, you should try driving my truck in the snow. I swear, the rear end on that thing is so light, the second we get even a dusting, I'm fishtailing all over the place. I tried putting a couple of sandbags in the bed last winter, but they got soaked and froze solid into these giant ice blocks. Took me until April to get them out. Spring was really late last year, too. I remember we had a freak snowstorm right around Easter. We had the whole family coming over for a ham dinner, and my brother-in-law got his Honda stuck at the end of my driveway. He's not the best driver to begin with, honestly. He always rides the brakes. I rode with him to a Bruins game once and I swear I was carsick before we even hit the highway. We had decent seats, though, right behind the penalty box...

Wait, sorry. I keep doing that, don't I? But yeah, no, I don't really think about it like getting control back. I just don't want a fire.
Do you feel like the electrical panels or your work need to be arranged in a specific way for you to consider them complete?

No, not really. Like I was saying before, I don't care if it looks a certain way or if it's perfectly neat. As long as it's safe and up to code, I'm good. I mean, some guys, they spend hours making sure every wire is bent at a perfect ninety-degree angle, and it looks like a piece of art when they're done. 

There's this guy I work with sometimes, Dave, he's exactly like that. He'll spend an extra hour on a panel just making it look pretty. But Dave's always been a little particular. He won't even eat a sandwich if the crusts aren't cut off. We went to this deli near a job site a few weeks ago—great pastrami, by the way, they pile it like three inches high—and he actually asked the lady behind the counter to trim the crusts off his rye bread. She looked at him like he had two heads. I usually just get the turkey club, but they use that thick-cut bacon, and it's always so crispy. I try not to eat too much bacon anymore, though. My doctor told me my cholesterol was creeping up at my last physical. He told me to start eating oatmeal for breakfast. I tried it for a week, but it just tastes like wet cardboard, you know? I tried putting brown sugar and raisins in it, but then I'm just eating a bowl of sugar, which kind of defeats the purpose, I think. 

Anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the panels. Yeah, no, I don't need them arranged any special way. Just safe.
Do you feel like the electrical panels or any part of your work needs to be symmetrical or have a specific order for you to feel okay about it?

I feel like we just talked about this, Doc. No, I don't care if it's symmetrical or whatever. I don't need the wires to look like a rainbow or be perfectly spaced out. I just need to know it's not going to spark and burn the house down. That's it. 

Speaking of burning things down, though, my neighbor almost set his deck on fire last weekend. He bought one of those fancy pellet smokers, you know, the ones that cost like a thousand bucks and have an app on your phone? He was trying to smoke a brisket overnight, and I guess the auger jammed or something, and the pellets backed up into the hopper. Next thing you know, there's smoke billowing out of the thing like a freight train. I saw it from my kitchen window when I got up to get a glass of water. I ran over there in my slippers and had to spray it down with his garden hose. Ruined a perfectly good piece of meat, too. Brisket is so expensive right now, it's crazy. I went to the butcher shop down on Main Street—the one with the sawdust on the floor, you know the place?—and they wanted like eight bucks a pound for a packer brisket. I told the guy he was out of his mind. I ended up just getting some Italian sausages instead. They make them in-house, sweet and hot. I like to grill them up with some peppers and onions on a nice crusty roll...

Man, I'm making myself hungry. But yeah, no, symmetry? Don't care. Just the safety stuff.
Is your need to check things over and over driven more by the fear of missing something that could cause a problem, or by the desire to make sure everything is perfect?

Oh, definitely the fear of missing something. Like I said, I don't care about perfect at all. It's just... even after I know I checked a panel or a disconnect, this thought just keeps barging in on me that maybe I missed one loose neutral, you know? Or that I left something exposed that could start a fire. I try to shake it off, I really do, but it just follows me all the way home. 

Speaking of the drive home, the traffic on Route 9 has been absolutely brutal lately. They've had it down to one lane near the overpass since last October. It was supposed to be a six-week project, but you know how the state works. I hit a pothole there on Tuesday that practically swallowed my front right tire. Had to take the truck into the shop to get the alignment checked. The guy at the garage—Tony, I've been going to him for years, we actually played Pop Warner football together back in the day—he told me he's seeing like five cars a day with bent rims just from that one stretch of road. Tony's a great mechanic, but he's a die-hard Yankees fan, which is pretty rough to deal with around here. He actually has a piece of one of the old Yankee Stadium seats sitting right in his waiting room. I told him he's gonna scare away paying customers with that thing. He just laughed and told me to charge more for my electrical work so I can afford better tires...

Anyway, sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? But yeah, to answer your question, it's not about making it perfect. It's just that nagging thought about a fire following me around.
Is your repetitive checking of work mostly because you're afraid of making a specific mistake, like causing a fire, or is it more because you feel anxious if you don't check everything?

It's the specific mistake, definitely the fire thing. That's actually what brings me in here, honestly. I just keep going back over my jobs again and again to make sure I didn't cause a hazard. I'll be checking the breakers, reading the labels, looking at my torque marks... I even started taking photos of the panels on my phone to prove to myself it's fine. But sometimes even the photos aren't enough, and I'll literally drive all the way back to a site after I've left just to look at it one more time. 

I did that on Tuesday at this big colonial house over in Westover. The homeowner had this massive Golden Retriever, Bailey I think her name was, who just jumped on everyone. Sweet dog, but she shed like crazy. I had blonde dog hair all over my dark work pants for two days. I buy those lint rollers in bulk at Costco—you know, the ones with the extra sticky tape? They come in a five-pack, but honestly, I go through them so fast I should probably just buy stock in the company. Costco is great, though. You can't beat their rotisserie chickens for five bucks. I usually grab one on my way home if I'm too tired to cook. They put them right in the back of the store so you have to walk past all the TVs and electronics, which is exactly how they get you. I almost bought a 65-inch Samsung last month when I just went in for chicken and paper towels. It was on sale, but my wife would have killed me if I came home with another TV... 

Anyway, sorry. But yeah, because I keep doing all this checking and driving back, a simple install ends up taking me way longer than it should. It's getting bad, and people at work are definitely starting to notice that I'm dragging my feet on these jobs.

Sal's a great guy, salt of the earth. He's been working on my cars since I got my license. His shop is over by the old abandoned paper mill. He said he might have to pull one from a salvage yard in upstate New York. I told him, Sal, I can't be without my truck for a week, I've got tools in there, I've got... 

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? But yeah, to answer your question, it's causing me a ton of distress. The whole thing is just exhausting.

Takes an absolute beating but it's perfect for the shallow water out at Lake Miller. Though last time I took it out, the outboard motor was acting up. Kept sputtering every time I gave it some throttle. I'm pretty sure the carburetor is gummed up. I learned that the hard way back when I had my first dirt bike, a Yamaha YZ125. Man, that thing was fast. I wiped out on a gravel road once and scraped all the skin off my left forearm, my mom was absolutely furious... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Right, daily life. But yeah, my daily life is basically just working, checking, and worrying. It's really no way to live.

Fires are no joke. I always tell my clients to make sure they're testing their smoke detectors, but nobody ever changes the batteries. You're supposed to do it when the clocks change. I actually just went to Costco to buy a huge pack of 9-volts for my own house. Man, I love Costco, but you go in there for batteries and come out with a $300 receipt. Last time I went, they had these massive inflatable paddleboards right in the center aisle. I almost bought one, but then I remembered I don't even like swimming in the ocean. The water around here is way too cold anyway, even in August. My wife and I went to Cape Cod a few years ago and the water was absolutely freezing, plus there are all those great white sharks they keep spotting off the coast now. They have an app that tracks them, actually, and you can see...

Wait, sorry, I'm rambling again. But yeah, that's the main fear. I'm just terrified I'll make a mistake that burns a house down, and the thought just won't leave me alone.

Even when I know for a fact I checked the disconnect, that fear of leaving something that could spark and start a fire just follows me all the way home. 

Speaking of the drive home, they've been doing all this road work on Route 9, and it is a complete nightmare. They've had the right lane closed for, what, three months now? And the potholes... I hit one so hard last Tuesday I thought I bent a rim on the truck. Tires aren't cheap either, especially the heavy-duty all-terrains I have to buy because some of these new residential construction sites are just pure mud. Took me a solid month to break them in, and I had just treated the leather with this mink oil my grandfather used to swear by. He was a cobbler, actually, had a little shop downtown next to the old movie theater before they tore it down to build that pharmacy...

Wait, sorry. I'm way off track again. But no, it's not about perfection at all. It's just that specific fear of a loose wire and a fire.

We got this new mattress, one of those memory foam things they ship to you in a box. It's crazy how they vacuum seal it down that small. You cut the plastic and it just inflates like a life raft. My wife loves it, but I feel like I'm sinking into quicksand every night. It gets so hot, too. I end up kicking the blankets off by 2 AM. We used to have a regular spring mattress, had it for like fifteen years, and honestly, I slept way better on that old thing. I tried to tell her we should just flip it, but she said it was sagging...

Uh, what was the question? Order and symmetry? Yeah, no, I don't care about that stuff on the job. Just the fire thing.

Spring was really late last year, too. I remember we had a freak snowstorm right around Easter. He always rides the brakes. I rode with him to a Bruins game once and I swear I was carsick before we even hit the highway. We had decent seats, though, right behind the penalty box...

Wait, sorry. I keep doing that, don't I? But yeah, no, I don't really think about it like getting control back. I just don't want a fire.

He won't even eat a sandwich if the crusts aren't cut off. She looked at him like he had two heads. I usually just get the turkey club, but they use that thick-cut bacon, and it's always so crispy. I try not to eat too much bacon anymore, though. My doctor told me my cholesterol was creeping up at my last physical. He told me to start eating oatmeal for breakfast. I tried it for a week, but it just tastes like wet cardboard, you know? I tried putting brown sugar and raisins in it, but then I'm just eating a bowl of sugar, which kind of defeats the purpose, I think.

Sweet dog, but she shed like crazy. I had blonde dog hair all over my dark work pants for two days. I buy those lint rollers in bulk at Costco—you know, the ones with the extra sticky tape?
